name: ECH and DoH visibility
plain: Encrypted Client Hello and DNS over HTTPS hide which site a visitor connects to from the local network.
meaning: ECH encrypts the SNI and the rest of the ClientHello using a key from DNS HTTPS records (RFC 9849 in Chrome 117 and Firefox 118 era). DoH encrypts DNS lookups. They hide hostnames from ISPs but not from the site, and they weaken JA3/JA4 on the wire.

web.api: TLS ECH extension; HTTPS RR; DoH

steps: Network sees only a public name

limits.headline: Can hide the site you visit from your internet provider, not from the site itself
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser can turn it on by itself, or you choose it in settings
can: Hide the site name from your internet provider on supported sites
Hide your DNS lookups from your network with secure DNS
Keep working on supported sites without changing how pages look
cannot: Hide you from the site you visit; it still sees you connect
Work with some network filters and monitors, which may break or block it
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Samsung Internet support it. Safari does not yet.

story.what_it_is: Hides which site you connect to from people watching your network.

marketing.name: Encrypted Client Hello
marketing.pitch: Cloudflare pitches it as the missing piece that hides which website you visit from anyone watching the connection.

marketing.name: DNS over HTTPS
marketing.pitch: Mozilla describes DNS over HTTPS as a way to encrypt website lookups so others on the network cannot see them.

story.for_you: You see nothing change. On public Wi-Fi or at a school, the network can no longer easily see which site you are opening. Your home network or work can still see that you connected.
story.for_makers: Makers get stronger privacy for visitors and fewer blocked connections. Network filters, schools and countries lose an easy way to block sites by name. Some security tools also lose visibility.

use_cases.example: A news site in a country with censorship becomes harder for the network to block by name.
A gamer on school or hotel Wi-Fi opens a game site that the network blocks by name, and it still loads.
A company security tool loses sight of which sites staff open, so it uses managed browsers instead.
A shopper on cafe Wi-Fi hides which stores they visit from nearby snoopers.
Internet providers lose a data source used to sell browsing history to marketers.
A researcher measures how much web traffic hides its destination.

technical_bounds: Needs an ECH enabled CDN (Cloudflare) and DoH
Outer SNI still visible as a shared public name
